walkthroughs.body_html:
Producing Robust Programs — a core area of GCSE Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Producing Robust Programs brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Producing Robust Programs.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A range check is an example of:
options: Input validation
Authentication
Compression
Defragmentation
Values at the very edge of the acceptable range
Values chosen completely at random
Only letters and symbols
Data that crashes the compiler

mcqs.q: A program that runs without crashing but produces the wrong answer contains:
options: A logic error
A syntax error
A hardware fault
No error at all

mcqs.q: Which of these improves the maintainability of a program?
options: Comments, sensible variable names and indentation
Removing all spaces from the code
Naming every variable x
Deleting all subprograms

mcqs.q: Does passing all its tests prove a program has no bugs?
options: Yes - one successful run with normal data proves correctness.
Yes - a full pass means the program is certified bug-free.
No - testing can show the presence of errors but never their complete absence; untested paths and unanticipated inputs can still hide bugs.
Yes - validation checks data against official records.

mcqs.q: Does validation guarantee the data entered is true?
options: Yes - validated data is always accurate.
No - validation only confirms data is reasonable and within the rules; a user can type a wrong but valid value, which is why verification exists.
Yes - validation checks data against official records.
Yes - defensive design only matters for games.

mcqs.q: If users follow the instructions, is defensive design unnecessary?
options: Yes - defensive design only matters for games.
No - defensive design exists precisely because real users make mistakes and attackers deliberately misuse programs; robust code assumes bad input will arrive.
Yes - one successful run with normal data proves correctness.
Yes - well-written instructions remove the need for validation.
